name: Nhuom rang (Vietnamese tooth dyeing)

lead:
Nhuộm răng is the Vietnamese tradition of dyeing the teeth black. For centuries many Kinh Vietnamese and several ethnic minorities treated glossy black teeth as the beautiful, adult look, with white teeth associated with animals or outsiders.
The custom was usually carried out around puberty to mark adulthood. It declined through the twentieth century with French colonial and Western influence and is now seen mainly among elderly women, although some younger women have revived it or use artificial blackened teeth.

paras: Historical accounts describe a preparation of the mouth followed by repeated applications of dark substances, such as burnt coconut shell, shellac-based pastes or iron-containing solutions, sometimes over several days. Deeper black was favored by girls and married women, while men often chose a lighter tone.

Accounts note that the process was painful and could leave the gums swollen. Modern dental views are not well documented, and the custom is distinguished in encyclopedic accounts from betel chewing, which is linked to tooth and gum damage.

angle.text: Within traditional Vietnamese beauty standards the black color was the goal: it was admired on girls and married women as a sign of beauty and maturity. It illustrates how ideals of the ideal smile differ across cultures and eras.

lead: Nhuộm răng, Vietnamese tooth blackening or lacquering, is a traditional body-modification custom in which the teeth are dyed a lustrous black. In Vietnam it was practiced by the majority Kinh population and by several minority groups, and black teeth were seen as an attractive, mature and civilized look.[1][2]

Archaeological remains at the Núi Nấp site suggest the practice existed by about 400 BCE. Foreign visitors from the 12th to 17th centuries describe black-toothed Vietnamese, and a 1692 Korean record mentions envoys with black teeth.[1] In the 1920s most women in Hanoi were reported to have blackened teeth.[1][2]

Under Western and French colonial influence the custom declined generation by generation. It is now chiefly seen among older women, and some younger women still practice it or wear artificial black teeth.[1]

paras: Tooth blackening is described as a rite of passage in parts of Asia and Oceania, most notably Japan and Vietnam, often marking entry into adulthood.[2] In Vietnam the preferred shade differed by group: deep black for girls and married women, lighter for men.[1]

Archaeological evidence from Núi Nấp points to blackened teeth around 400 BCE in the Đông Sơn era.[1] During the Ming occupation, officials ordered Vietnamese to stop the custom as part of what they called civilizing the population, and the later emperor Quang Trung is recorded as invoking black teeth as a symbol of resistance in a pre-battle address.[1][2]
A colonial-era medical report of the 1930s claimed that about 80 percent of Tonkinese farmers had darkened teeth, and the practice faded across the twentieth century.[1]

Descriptions mention cleaning the mouth with a mix of dried betel, charcoal powder and salt, then rinsing with rice wine and lemon juice before applying dye such as burnt coconut shell or an iron-based solution; an older text describes shellac paste followed by black alum.[1] The process is described as painful because it can swell the gums.[1]

Black teeth signified beauty, maturity and refinement, and were contrasted with the white teeth of animals and outsiders.[1][2] In Japan the equivalent custom, ohaguro, used iron acetate and tannins and was banned in 1870.[2]
